title: Vascular Disease • PAD, Acute Occlusion, Aneurysm, Carotid Stenosis
source_note: Generalized from teaching notes; no copyrighted verbatim.

items.question: Classic symptom pattern of intermittent claudication from aortoiliac disease includes pain where?
options: Calf with walking, relieved by rest
Buttock/hip with exertion, relieved by rest, ± impotence
Shoulder pain radiating to arm with exertion
Diffuse leg cramping at night only
items.rationale: Aortoiliac occlusive disease classically causes buttock/hip claudication and may cause impotence (Leriche-like pattern).

items.question: Which physical finding is most consistent with chronic PAD of the lower limb?
options: Warm, hyperemic skin and bounding pulses
Cool skin, hair loss, diminished or absent distal pulses
Brown hemosiderin staining around ankles with strong pulses
items.rationale: PAD reduces distal perfusion leading to cool skin, trophic changes (hair loss), and decreased pulses.

items.question: Nonhealing toe ulcers and pain at rest most suggest disease of which arterial segment?
items.rationale: Fem-pop disease commonly progresses to rest pain and distal ischemic ulcers, especially on toes/trauma points.

items.question: Bedside test that estimates PAD severity and follows perfusion after interventions is:
items.rationale: ABI tracks limb perfusion; significant drops (e.g., ≥0.15) warrant concern post-revascularization.

items.question: Which imaging modality can screen for and localize arterial occlusive lesions noninvasively?
items.rationale: Duplex and Doppler assess flow and stenosis; arteriography is more definitive when intervention is planned.

items.question: Initial activity advice during an acute limb ischemia flare is to:
options: Encourage walking through the pain to improve collaterals
Immediately cease activity and rest; protect from trauma and maintain normothermia
Ice the extremity to reduce swelling
items.rationale: During acute ischemic exacerbations, reduce oxygen demand and avoid injury while definitive therapy proceeds.

items.question: Which drug class is routinely used long-term in PAD to reduce atherothrombotic events?
items.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy lowers risk of CV events in atherosclerotic disease, including PAD.

items.question: Cilostazol may be considered in PAD primarily to:
options: Improve claudication walking distance via vasodilation and antiplatelet effects
items.rationale: As a PDE III inhibitor, cilostazol improves walking distance; not a substitute for revascularization when indicated.

items.question: Key post–endovascular fem-pop stent nursing priority is:
options: Aggressive hip flexion to reduce back pain
Tight limb wrapping to increase venous return
Frequent neurovascular checks and access-site monitoring for bleeding/hematoma
items.rationale: After percutaneous interventions, monitor for access complications and distal perfusion (the 6 Ps).

items.question: Recommended leg positioning in early post–lower-extremity bypass to protect graft flow typically avoids:
options: Ankle pumps and gentle foot exercises
items.rationale: Flexion and crossing can kink/pressure the graft; gentle movement without compression is preferred.

items.question: The '6 Ps' of acute limb ischemia include: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and:
items.rationale: Coldness (poikilothermia/polar) reflects absent perfusion in acute occlusion.

items.question: Best immediate limb positioning for acute arterial occlusion is to keep the limb:
options: Elevated above heart with ice packs
Compressed with a tight elastic wrap
items.rationale: Dependency and warmth optimize any residual flow; avoid compression/ice that reduce perfusion further.

items.question: Which scenario most strongly suggests an embolic source of acute limb ischemia?
options: Gradually worsening calf pain over months
Sudden severe leg pain and pallor in patient with atrial fibrillation
items.rationale: Afib predisposes to arterial emboli lodging in distal vessels, causing abrupt ischemia.

items.question: First-line reperfusion options for eligible acute arterial occlusion include:
items.rationale: Time-critical limb salvage uses catheter-directed lysis or surgical embolectomy depending on anatomy and viability.

items.question: While preparing for angiography, essential nursing actions include all EXCEPT:
options: Administer oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥95% unless contraindicated
Keep limb cool and elevated high
Provide analgesia and notify provider immediately of perfusion deficit
items.rationale: Avoid cooling/elevation that decrease arterial inflow; keep limb dependent and warm.

items.question: Definition of an aortic aneurysm is a localized aortic dilation of at least:
items.rationale: Aneurysm is typically defined as ≥1.5× the expected normal diameter for that segment.

items.question: Sudden tearing chest or back pain with pulse/BP differentials between limbs most suggests:
items.rationale: Dissection classically causes abrupt severe pain and asymmetric pulses/BP by branch involvement.

items.question: Chest radiograph clue that raises suspicion for thoracic aortic pathology is:
items.rationale: A widened mediastinum can indicate dissection/aneurysm but requires definitive imaging.

items.question: Initial BP/HR management in suspected aortic dissection prioritizes:
options: Vasodilator first to drop BP then consider beta-blockade
Beta-blocker first to reduce shear (HR/dP-dt), then add vasodilator
items.rationale: Shear reduction with beta-blockade precedes arterial vasodilation to avoid reflex tachycardia.

items.question: Indications that often prompt repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm include diameter roughly:
items.rationale: Risk–benefit commonly favors repair around 5–6 cm or if rapid growth/symptoms; patient-specific factors apply.

items.question: Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR/TEVAR) advantages vs open repair include:
options: Lower early morbidity and shorter stay in appropriate anatomy
No need for any follow-up imaging
Suitable regardless of vessel size/neck anatomy
items.rationale: EVAR has lower early morbidity but requires lifelong surveillance; anatomy must be suitable.

items.question: Post-repair complication unique to endovascular grafts is:
options: Endoleak with persistent pressurization of aneurysm sac
items.rationale: Endoleak represents blood flow outside the graft lumen but within aneurysm sac; may need re-intervention.

items.question: Target hemodynamics in dissection often aim for MAP around:
options: 60–75 mm Hg if tolerated to reduce shear (with close perfusion monitoring)
>120 mm Hg to maintain organ flow
items.rationale: Controlled hypotension reduces aortic wall stress; balance with end-organ perfusion and clinical status.

items.question: Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) is most consistent with emboli from:
options: Internal carotid artery ipsilateral to the affected eye
items.rationale: Amaurosis fugax reflects retinal ischemia typically from ipsilateral internal carotid disease.

items.question: First-line noninvasive test for suspected carotid stenosis is:
items.rationale: Carotid duplex is initial; advanced imaging is reserved when results are nondiagnostic or for planning.

items.question: Medical therapy cornerstone to reduce stroke risk in carotid atherosclerosis includes:
items.rationale: Antiplatelets plus risk-factor modification (BP, lipids, DM, tobacco) reduce vascular events.

items.question: A typical interventional threshold for symptomatic high-grade internal carotid stenosis is roughly:
items.rationale: Symptomatic high-grade stenosis (~≥70%) may benefit from CEA or stenting if surgical risk acceptable.

items.question: Immediate post–carotid endarterectomy priorities include:
options: Keep patient flat with neck flexed
Watch for neck hematoma and airway compromise; frequent neuro checks and BP control
Avoid any BP monitoring for 24 h
items.rationale: Neck hematoma threatens the airway; neuro checks and tight BP control mitigate hypoperfusion/hemorrhage risks.

items.question: Cranial nerve deficits can occur after open carotid surgery. Which bedside screen is relevant?
options: Ask patient to smile, shrug, swallow, and protrude tongue
items.rationale: Quick checks include CN VII (smile), IX/X (swallow/speech/gag), XI (shrug), XII (tongue midline).

items.question: Compared with carotid stenting, open endarterectomy more commonly risks:
items.rationale: CEA carries cranial nerve injury risk; stenting avoids that specific risk but has others (e.g., embolic events).
